AJK.name: Juneau
AJK.excerpt: The strongest of these systems is expected to be the initial front moving through on Monday into Tuesday, especially across the southern panhandle, bringing gale force winds up Clarence Strait.

sections.name: Update
paragraphs: Aviation update with the 18Z TAF issuance. No major changes in the short term forecast, with the exception of fog remaining over Juneau this morning, predominantly over the airport and valley areas. This will linger longer than anticipated even with the sun being out, and will gradually lift late morning into the early afternoon. Some patchy fog may remain even as areas begin to clear up.

sections.name: Synopsis
paragraphs: - Offshore flow allows for northerly winds and drier conditions through Sunday.

- A stronger low pressure system moves north into the southeastern Gulf of Alaska Monday, increasing winds across the southern inner channels and the offshore Gulf of Alaska coastal waters into Tuesday.
- An associated front with the Gulf of Alaska low pressure system moves into the southern Panhandle Monday increasing rain chances Monday into Tuesday.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Ridging over the eastern gulf and panhandle in place Sunday and holding to the start of the week. Mostly sunny daytime skies, and localized lower stratus deck in parts of the central panhandle that formed over night. And may see some fog developing again for a couple of hours but do not think it will be widespread or last for hours. Expect to see rain to start spreading north over the panhandle Monday with low chances and by afternoon, categorical rain. Late monday and into early tuesday the chances have reached the northern sections. With the cooler temperatures there and high elevations, and locations away from the open water channels, may see a mix or a snow start in those locations, however am not expecting accumulations of any significance.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: /Tuesday through Thursday/...Active weather ensues headed into mid week as the aforementioned system moves north across the panhandle. An initial front is expected to move across the panhandle Monday night into Tuesday morning bringing light to periods of moderate rain. As mentioned in the short term discussion, communities across the northern panhandle could see a wintry mix at the onset of the front, but incoming cloud cover could prevent temperatures from reaching low enough for frozen precipitation to ensue. Precipitation chances along the north gulf coast stay relatively low through Tuesday with this front potentially dying out or passing through just south of the area. Models are still split on the exact timing of the next front with the Canadian and European models bringing rain up from the south Tuesday morning, but the GFS has rain moving in Tuesday afternoon to evening. The GFS then indicates more of a break on Wednesday before a third front moves in, with the Canadian and the European giving little to no respite between waves of rain. Rain continues through the day Thursday as well as another front moves across the area.

The strongest of these systems is expected to be the initial front moving through on Monday into Tuesday, especially across the southern panhandle, bringing gale force winds up Clarence Strait. Winds are anticipated to remain elevated through the day Tuesday before diminishing Wednesday. The pressure gradient is likely to then become the main driver of wind for the rest of the period as a east/west pressure gradient sets up across the panhandle.

BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: Forecast guidance becomes increasingly messy by the weekend, with several solutions favoring active and unsettled weather with lingering precipitation.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Light valley rain and mountain snow expected through Monday afternoon.
- A generally unsettled pattern will continue through next week, with brief dry periods.
- Late week unsettled weather will come alongside warmer temps and higher snow levels.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Troughing along the West Coast will keep a chance of light precipitation over the region through Monday morning. A shortwave trough pushing onto the central CA coast will lift through the Great Basin and southern Idaho tonight. Precipitation coverage will increase across in response to this passing wave, with a path of light rain/snow from far SE Oregon through the central ID mtns. Snow levels will hold around 4kft with accumulating snow above 4.5kft MSL. Higher terrain south of the Snake Plain and along the OR/NV border will see less than an inch. North of the Snake Plain totals will range between 1-3 inches in the Boise/Soldier mtns with less than 2 inches to the north. Clearing skies Monday morning will lead to areas of fog development in lower valleys/basins of SE Oregon and the lower Snake. Not confident on dense fog formation but certainly surface moisture is present and winds will be light so it's a possibility.

A shortwave ridge transitions across the area tonight into Tuesday bringing a brief break in the precipitation. The next upper wave pushes into the Pac NW late Tuesday, increasing precipitation chances across SE Oregon Tuesday night. Similar to recent storms models depict the parent low remaining near shore while a weakened shortwave trough tracks through the Interior NW. This will result in light rain/snow amounts with snow levels generally 4-5kft MSL Tuesday night. High temperatures are near normal Monday, warming to around 5 degrees above normal Tuesday.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: A strong upper low off the coast of British Columbia stalls for the early part of the long term forecast. Despite the upper low stalling, a surface low collides with the coast. Initially the low produces efficient precipitation over the Cascades, but with the upper low stalled: the surface low loses steam as it arrives to our forecast area. A weak shortwave is all that remains when it moves overhead Wednesday evening, producing light isolated precipitation if anything. This initial slow progression will allow a high pressure ridge to build up through the Great Basin. By Thursday through Saturday that high pressure brings temps up to 5-10 degrees above normal and allows snow levels to climb up to 6-8 kft MSL. Just as that ridge develops, the upper low is finally ready to move east along the US-Canada border. Widespread precipitation is expected late Thursday through early Saturday, falling almost entirely as rain except for mountains above 6kft MSL. The best chance for snow in mountain valleys will be in the earliest hours of the precip Thursday evening before snow levels rise. Additionally, the zonal flow between the low and the ridge will support gusty conditions in open areas and ridgelines. There is still some uncertainty on where exactly the precipitation tracks late in the week, with a few ensemble members showing an amplified ridge pushing precip north. If this high pressure effectively keeps most of the moisture and zonal flow to the north, inversion concerns with low stratus and fog in the Snake River Valley could return by late week.

Forecast guidance becomes increasingly messy by the weekend, with several solutions favoring active and unsettled weather with lingering precipitation. All model solutions depict some form of another upper level trough or closed low by Sunday, with widely varying storm tracks and impacts for the region. Current forecast favors a 30-50% chance of precipitation for lower elevations, with better confidence for high terrain in Idaho with a 50-70% chance of measurable precipitation.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: Upper-level ridging creeps its way back into Colorado Wednesday as the axis should be centered across our area by the afternoon. Ensemble guidance is in good agreement this will induce gradual warming through the weekend.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Patchy freezing fog possible for lincoln and eastern Elbert counties Monday morning.
- A system brings a chance for light mountain snow showers late Monday into Tuesday morning.
- Cooler fall temperatures to continue through mid next week.
- No major travel impacts are expected during the Thanksgiving travel period.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Current satellite imagery shows high clouds trekking across the NE plains of Colorado. The upper air pattern features slight ridging aloft as we wait for the shortwave to move in off the coast of California. Temperatures this afternoon across the South Platte River valley may only reach the lower 40s compared to mid/upper 40s in the Denver metro as a result of this mornings fog and low clouds. A Denver cyclone will develop today and coupled with southerly downsloping winds off the Palmer Divide, generate breezy conditions for Elbert, Lincoln, and areas east of DIA. Low temperatures for the next few nights will reach the 20s with valleys and naturally colder spots approaching the upper teens. Freezing fog is also possible Monday morning for Lincoln and eastern Elbert counties. Reduced visiblities down to 0.25-0.50 sm are possible.

Ensemble and deterministic models are in good agreement for a shortwave to move across the Central Rockies tomorrow. This system should bring enough lift and moisture to the mountains to produce our next chance of snow for the higher terrain (40-60%). Snowfall is likely to accumulate in the Mosquito Range, Gore Range, with lighter accumulations across the Continental Divide and Front Range. Snow will start Monday afternoon before tapering off early Tuesday morning. The greatest accumulation's appear to be focused on the Gore and Mosquito ranges, where the probability of 24 hr snowfall >1" is 60-70% and >2" is ~40-50%. Portions of the Palmer Divide and Lincoln county still have a ~10-20% chance to see measurable snowfall. Due to the expected cloud cover tomorrow, forecasted high temperatures should remain in the lower 40s for most of the area. Tuesday's sky will clear with cool high temperatures once again in the upper 40s.

Upper-level ridging creeps its way back into Colorado Wednesday as the axis should be centered across our area by the afternoon. Ensemble guidance is in good agreement this will induce gradual warming through the weekend. Thanksgiving day looks to be mild in the 50s and dry with no impactful weather. Ensembles for the weekend depict a large high pressure to develop over the western coast causing NW flow aloft for the weekend. This NW direction will lead to upslope flow for the northern and central mountains which may produce periods of snow showers. Ensembles are in disagreement regarding the location of jets and other factors that could influence snowfall amounts. For now this will be something to just keep an eye on. However, our lower elevations are looking likely to stay dry through this weekend.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Models are still trending with the split flow regime centered over the Intermountain West. Which means the chance for any precipitation is likely to fade quickly for the long term forecast.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Chilly temperatures will continue through Tuesday.
- Marginally high winds will be possible Tuesday night for the wind prone areas of southeast Wyoming.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Fog from this morning has lifted across the eastern plains with some remnant low clouds east of Interstate 25 early this afternoon. Visible Satellite loop shows another round of mid to high clouds moving eastward across the area, which should help in keeping afternoon temperatures relatively cool for this time of the year and generally in the 30s. Lows tonight should be a few degrees warmer due to the cloud cover, but will likely drop into the upper teens to mid 20s due to light winds. Another tricky fog forecast for tonight with dew point depressions remaining relatively low this afternoon. Added some patchy freezing fog to east central Wyoming and portions of the North Platte River Valley from Douglas to near Torrington. Kept the areal coverage of fog in the same general vicinity as high res ensemble probabilities, which show around a 30% chance in these areas. Can't rule out the southern panhandle either, but probabilities are much lower compared to the last several nights.

For the start of the work week, models indicate a transient shortwave ridge axis translating eastward over the region in the morning as the next poorly defined upper level trough moves into the eastern Great Basin Region and eventually into the Front Range Monday evening. Mainly dry conditions are expected as the trough axis moves across the area with some snow showers developing over the mountains later on Monday. Any snow accumulations should be less than an inch in the mountains with little, if any, impacts. Below average temperatures will continue with highs struggling to reach 40 degrees for most locations under mostly cloudy skies. Temperatures will start to warm up a bit on Tuesday behind the upper level trough, which will continue to track eastward into the Great Plains. Dry conditions will continue on Tuesday with windy conditions developing over southeast Wyoming, mainly along and west of the I-25 corridor.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Models are still trending with the split flow regime centered over the Intermountain West. Which means the chance for any precipitation is likely to fade quickly for the long term forecast. A weak area of high pressure will essentially wobble around the Intermountain West as Low pressure systems move across the southern United states and the Canadian providences. Temperatures will increase slightly throughout the work week. Tuesday temperatures will be a little cooler in the upper 40's with the temperature climbing to the mid 50's by Thursday. These warmer temperatures don't come to us free of charge though. Our ridge begins to break down slightly as a couple upper level lows begin to move across the Canadian Providences before diving through the Northern Plains by Friday. The first system begins to dive Wednesday afternoon increasing our cloud cover and start the increase of winds in the afternoon. This sets the stage for a potential high wind event starting late Thursday evening and eventually ending Friday night into early Saturday morning. The major cause of our high winds will be the second upper level low transversing a little more south into Montana and the Dakotas placing the jetstream right over Wyoming. Some models (AI-GFS) may be overdoing the winds a touch but it gets the point across. Thanksgiving will be generally warm for this time of year with temperatures in the low 50's with the winds slowly increasing throughout the evening as family wind down from the holiday festivities. Thursday night into Friday morning the Low pressure system will make its presence known as it further compresses the height gradient over the Southeast Wyoming region. The Craig to Casper gradient looks to jump from 31 meters to 73 meters around 11PM Thursday to 1 AM Friday. Looking at the global omega fields, maxed out subsident values followed by strong rising motion give support to the mountain wave/high wind ideology. Friday afternoon looks to be the peak of the mountain wave intensity as the 700mb jet climbs to about 65 to 70 knots. By Friday evening and into the overnight hours the winds will gradually calm down to our normal Wyoming breezy levels. The plus side will be that due to the downsloping winds it will be a 50/50 day Friday(50 mph winds and afternoon temperatures in the 50's).

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: By Tuesday morning, the trough will move east of our area, and ridging builds in. Conditions through Wednesday are expected to be dry with temperatures remaining near or slightly below normal.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Generally dry and cooler conditions return for Sunday.
- A quick moving system will bring areas of rain and snow showers for Monday.
- Active weather remains possible for Thanksgiving week, but some details still remain uncertain. Stay tuned for updates to timing and impacts as they become available.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Dry and cool weather is expected for Sunday with a weak ridge moving through the Intermountain West. Mid to high level clouds will move in from the west through the day as our next storm system approaches.

Moisture will begin to move into the area Sunday night as a weak low- amplitude trough moves through and brings southwesterly flow. This system will be fast moving with moisture and lift remaining limited. High-res models begin to develop light showers Monday morning over the Four Corners. This will bring a rain/snow mix for valley locations with mostly snow expected in the higher terrain above 6000 ft. There are some pockets of weak instability that may develop Monday afternoon (SBCAPE 50-100 J/kg) over southwest Colorado creating the possibility of locally heavier snowfall. The best chance for accumulating snow remains over the San Juans but accumulations are expected to be mostly light and be below advisory levels.
DRY AGAIN MIDWEEK, ACTIVE WEATHER POSSIBLE FOR END OF THE WEEK:

By Tuesday morning, the trough will move east of our area, and ridging builds in. Conditions through Wednesday are expected to be dry with temperatures remaining near or slightly below normal. The rest of the forecast period may remain active with some deterministic guidance showing another weak system for Thanksgiving Day. Northwesterly flow will primarily bring impacts to the Park Range, but exact details are uncertain at this time. Another system is possible next weekend, but ensemble members are still showing significant disagreement. Stay tuned on potential impacts to holiday travel plans.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: Transitory ridging builds across the region into Wednesday, leading to dry conditions and warming temperatures.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Another quick moving weather system will bring light snow to the higher terrain tomorrow, along with passing showers for the plains through Monday night.
- Trending warmer and drier into the Thanksgiving Holiday Weekend.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Current water vapor imagery and upper air analysis has modest westerly flow aloft across the region, with yesterday's passing system continues out across the High Plains, as another eastern Pacific system is moving onshore across the Pacific Northwest Coast. Water vapor imagery is also indicating mid and high level moisture embedded within the flow aloft streaming across the Great Basin and into the Rockies at this time.

Latest model data is in good agreement with short wave energy ejecting off the parent Pacific Northwest system, translating across Intermountain West and Great Basin region tonight, which continues across the Rockies through the day tomorrow and into the High Plains tomorrow night. With that said, will continue to see increasing high clouds across the region through tonight, with increasing chances of precipitation along and west of the Continental Divide through the morning hours, as available moisture and uvv increase ahead of the system. Showers spread east across the high mountain valleys through the eastern mountains and across the eastern plains through afternoon and evening hours, as the uvv continues to translate east overnight. With the quick movement of the system, expected qpf remains light, with snowfall of 1 to 3 inches possible over and near the higher terrain, and the greatest amounts expected across the eastern San Juans and the southern Sangres, where orographics and the best forcing will be combined. While light snow is expected with showers crossing the plains, any accumulations look to spotty and light with the quick moving system.

Temperatures to remain at and below seasonal levels, with lows in the teens and 20s tonight and Monday night, and highs mainly in the 40s across the plains on Monday, with 20s, 30s and 40s across the higher terrain.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Transitory ridging builds across the region into Wednesday, leading to dry conditions and warming temperatures. Latest operational and ensemble model data coming into better agreement of more eastern Pacific energy splitting as it translates across the Intermountain West Thursday and Friday. This will keep the region in moderate northwest flow into the end of the Thanksgiving Holiday weekend, with chances of precipitation confined mainly to the Northern and Central Mtns, and temperatures remaining at or slightly above seasonal levels. However, will need to continue to monitor the potential for surface high pressure building across the Northern High Plains to send a backdoor cold front into eastern Colorado later next weekend.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: Model guidance continues to trend drier with a weak trough moving through late Wednesday into Thursday, but this thankfully means little to no impactful weather for holiday travel and enough mixing to ward off valley inversion development.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - A weak weather system will bring a chance of snow showers across higher terrain on Monday, with little accumulation.
- Low chances for fog development will return Tuesday morning across prone areas such as the Cache Valley, depending on if low clouds can fully clear out Monday night.
- Another weak system is forecast to cross the region on Thanksgiving. This will bring a small chance for valley rain and mountain snow to northern Utah, while southern Utah remains largely dry.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Mid- to upper-level clouds are in place this morning across much of Utah and southwest Wyoming with largely stable conditions and temperatures reaching just a few degrees below normal. As a fast-moving trough sweeps across the Great Basin tonight, modest moisture will gradually begin to infiltrate the lower levels, resulting in low precipitation chances on Monday primarily across higher terrain. Given weak dynamics and very limited moisture, rainfall/liquid equivalent will largely remain below 0.10" (90% chance).

An even drier air mass will move into the region following this storm system, with a ridge crossing the state Tuesday into Wednesday. Depending on how quickly low-level clouds are scoured out Monday night, fog-prone areas such as the Cache Valley could see patchy fog development by Tuesday morning given stable conditions, light winds, and potentially clearing skies. Otherwise, expect quiet weather through at least mid-week.

Model guidance continues to trend drier with a weak trough moving through late Wednesday into Thursday, but this thankfully means little to no impactful weather for holiday travel and enough mixing to ward off valley inversion development. Heading into this weekend, however, chances for precipitation will begin to increase. Forecast confidence is still low, as ultimately precipitation chances will depend on the trajectory of moisture from a landfalling atmospheric river in Oregon late this week. Currently, ensemble guidance appears to favor a more southwesterly trajectory which would result in moisture landing a bit too far north, but the deterministic GFS has a more zonal orientation, drawing moisture into northern Utah this weekend.

2660.travel_advice: Dangerous avalanche conditions. Careful snowpack evaluation, cautious route-finding and conservative decision-making essential.

product.author: Chris Dickson
bottom_line: You can trigger an avalanche large enough to bury you on steep, shady leeward slopes at upper elevations. You could also trigger avalanches from a distance, so give suspect slopes a wide buffer.
Wind-drifted slabs sit over weak snow on shady slopes from west to north to east near and above treeline. Safer travel can be found on lower-angled slopes and in wind-sheltered areas below treeline.

2753.travel_advice: Heightened avalanche conditions on specific terrain features. Evaluate snow and terrain carefully; identify features of concern.

product.author: Kreston Rohrig
bottom_line: Your chances of triggering an avalanche increase the higher you travel on the mountain, especially in previously wind-drifted areas. Use extra caution or simply avoid steeper slopes near and above treeline on northwest to north to east-facing slopes. There's a chance you could trigger a slope from a distance away, so be aware of other parties nearby.

2754.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Krista Beyer
bottom_line: Most slopes are generally safe from avalanches due to shallow or discontinuous snow cover. You might be able to trigger a small avalanche where recent winds have formed pockets of stiffened snow below ridgelines, on lee slopes, and around rocky outcrops in the alpine.

2745.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Andrew McWilliams
bottom_line: Snow cover is still too thin for avalanches on most slopes. In the alpine, you should steer around hard drifts of snow on steep terrain features and below ridgetops. Unfortunately, the slopes with enough snow to ride are also where you might find enough snow for slides.

3046.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

1736.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

3014.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Kevin Studley
bottom_line: Winter has begun to embrace the West Central Mountains of Idaho. 6-12 inches of new snow has fallen between Friday the 13th and Monday the 16th. Another 6-12 inches could stack up by the end of the week. If you're traveling in the mountains this week, watch out for wind slabs 1-2 feet thick above 7,000 feet and pay attention to terrain traps.
We'll update the General Avalanche Information weekly until full-time forecasting operations begin.
hazard_discussion: From 60-degree temperatures to over a foot of new snow, the weather sure has changed quickly over the past week. A cooler and wetter weather pattern has taken shape over our region since Friday the 13th. As of Monday (16th) afternoon, some mountain locations have picked up 6-12 inches of new snow along with southerly winds gusting 20-30 MPH.
Wind Slabs
• Wind slabs could become reactive this week with over a foot of new snow and gusty winds. Wind slabs will be most sensitive just below ridgelines.
• Look for clues of wind-affected snow, such as drifts, dunes, pillows, and freshly built cornices.
• Watch for signs of instability, such as shooting cracks. If you're observing these signs, find another aspect away from wind-drifted snow.
• Strong winds and local terrain features can alter the prevailing wind direction. Pay attention to cross-loading and wind-loading on unsuspecting slopes.
Early Season Conditions
• If you're out hiking or hunting in the mountains this fall, stay tuned to changing weather conditions. Avalanches are most likely during and immediately after a storm.

• Keep in mind the adage, "If there's enough snow to ride, there's enough snow to slide". Even if there's not enough snow to bury you, a small slide over uncovered logs, rocks, and brush would not be a fun way to start the season.
• Stay up to date on mountain weather with our WEATHER tab, where you'll find webcams, weather stations, and weather forecasting tools.
Check Your Winter Gear

• Beacons, shovels, probes, airbags. Run through all your gear and make sure it's functioning properly. Does your transceiver or airbag need any firmware updates? Look for cracks, defects, or corroded batteries. Make it fun with your friends and do a pre-season gear check with your winter travel companions.
Continuing Education
• Check out the Education tab on our website to sign up for avalanche courses this winter (COURSES ).
• Stay tuned to our EVENTS pages for other local happenings with the winter community.
• Interested in attending a snow and avalanche workshop (SAW)? Check out A3's WEBSITE for a list of events.
Observations
• Keep an eye on our observation page HERE

• If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation HERE. Early season observations help forecasters and the public alike. A simple photo and/or weather observation helps paint the picture of where snow is and where it is not.

Yeah, that's right: the Payette Avalanche Center has a new website. Browse around before the snow starts flying. We're also on the Avy App. You can search for "Avy: Avalanche & Weather Info" in your app store on your mobile device.

2755.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Andrew McWilliams
bottom_line: The snow cover is too thin for slides on most slopes, so avalanche danger is LOW. Recent snow drifts rest on weak, old snow. If you find a continuous drift of firm snow on a steep terrain feature, you can trigger a small slide. Steer around drifted pockets of snow where you see them below ridges or inside gullies.
